# v2.96

This stable release rolls up dev pre-releases v2.95-dev and v2.96-dev.

**There are no changes to the application in this release.** Everything below is
about how changes are made to Training Tracker and how releases reach you — the
software itself is functionally identical to v2.94. If you run an installation,
updating is safe and there is nothing to do afterwards.

It is published because the project's release process changed materially, and
that is worth being open about: it now has checks that a release has to pass
before it can be published, where previously it had almost none.

## Changed

- **Changes are now reviewed and tested before they are released, not after.**
  Previously, publishing a release was the act of saving the work: a change went
  out first and any problem with it surfaced afterwards. Now every change is
  proposed separately and has to pass a series of automated checks before it can
  become part of the product.

- **Every change is now built and checked automatically.** The checks run the
  same production build that runs when you update your own installation, along
  with code-quality and type checks, and a check that every part of the system
  that handles data still verifies who is asking. A failure stops the release.
  The most valuable of these is the build: it is the step that used to fail on
  *your* machine, part-way through an update, and it now fails on the project's
  own infrastructure instead.

- **The release checklist is now enforced rather than remembered.** Three things
  that were previously done by hand — advancing the version number correctly,
  keeping the dependency lock file in step, and writing the release notes you are
  reading — are verified automatically. A missed version number used to produce a
  release that silently contained nothing.

- **A privacy check now guards every change.** Training Tracker ships as a
  generic system, so the examples in its code, its documentation and its release
  notes must never contain real company names, real addresses, or anything
  identifying a real person. Each change is now scanned for that before it can be
  published, and anything found stops the release.

  The scan recognises patterns — addresses at unfamiliar domains, file paths
  naming a real account. It cannot recognise a real company, product or person's
  name, and deliberately does not try: checking for those automatically would
  mean keeping a list of them in the project, which is the very thing the rule
  exists to prevent. Those remain a human responsibility.

## Upgrading

Nothing to do. No database changes, no configuration changes, and no change to
the application. Update at your convenience.
